<div class="project-content">

<p class="lede-para">
  Built for the <strong>Grokathon</strong>. X Arcade is a retro arcade cabinet for X, and the first cartridge is
  <em>Decoy</em>: one real post, five replies, four written by people and one written by Grok. You have thirty seconds
  to spot the machine. It turns out that's much harder than it sounds — which is the whole point.
</p>

<div class="results">
  <div class="result"><span class="num">5</span><span class="lbl">Replies per round, one machine-written</span></div>
  <div class="result"><span class="num">30s</span><span class="lbl">To pick before the timer runs out</span></div>
  <div class="result"><span class="num">2</span><span class="lbl">Modes: fully offline demo, and live xAI</span></div>
</div>

<h2>The game</h2>

<ul>
  <li>Two players join the same room code from separate devices or tabs; the round starts the moment the second
  player joins.</li>
  <li>Everyone sees the same post and the same five replies. Tap the one you think the machine wrote.</li>
  <li>First correct pick takes the round, and the match continues from there.</li>
</ul>

<h2>The part that mattered: not failing on stage</h2>

<p>
  A hackathon demo that depends on live API calls is a demo that can die in front of the judges — rate limits, a slow
  response, conference wifi. So the architecture splits in two:
</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Demo mode</strong> (the default) runs on committed fixtures and pre-built assets with
  <strong>zero network calls</strong>. Rounds, host voice lines and the share card all ship in the repo, so the
  demo is deterministic and instant.</li>
  <li><strong>Live mode</strong> turns on real xAI calls behind an environment flag, and is treated strictly as an
  enhancement rather than a dependency.</li>
</ul>

<p>
  The same split makes the live features safe to add, because each one degrades instead of breaking:
</p>

<ul>
  <li><strong>Imagine</strong> — after the reveal, the share card is generated through the image API and re-broadcast
  when it lands (~6.5s). Demo mode serves the committed card immediately.</li>
  <li><strong>Voice</strong> — the browser mints a short-lived realtime token and opens a Grok voice session to speak
  the host cues. Any failure falls back to the committed audio files, so the host never goes silent.</li>
</ul>

<p>
  There's also a record flag that captures live responses back into the fixtures, so refreshing the offline demo
  assets is a single command rather than hand-editing JSON.
</p>

<h2>Deploying it</h2>

<p>
  Three deploy paths are committed, and the README is honest about the trade-off between them: Render on the free
  tier (what the live demo runs on — it sleeps after 15 minutes idle and takes about a minute to wake), Fly for
  always-on at a few dollars a month, and a Hugging Face Docker Space that needs a paid account. All three run in
  demo mode with no secrets attached.
</p>

<div class="note">
  <i class="bi bi-info-circle"></i>
  <p>The hosted demo sleeps when idle, so the first load can take about a minute to wake. Once a match is running
  it stays up.</p>
</div>
